blocks.p: Christiana then wished for an inn for herself and her children, because they were weary.
“There is one a little ahead of us,” said Mr. Honest, “where a very honorable disciple named Gaius lives.” [Rom. 16:23]

So they all agreed to turn in there, the more readily because the old gentleman gave him such a good report. When they came to the door they went straight in without knocking, since people don’t knock at the door of an inn. Then they called for the master of the house, and he came to them, and they asked whether they might stay the night.
“Yes, gentlemen, if you are true men,” said Gaius, “for my house is for pilgrims and no one else.”

At that Christiana, Mercy, and the boys were all the gladder, since the innkeeper was a lover of pilgrims. They called for rooms, and he showed them one for Christiana, her children, and Mercy, and another for Mr. Great-heart and the old gentleman.
“Good Gaius,” said Great-heart, “what have you for supper? These pilgrims have come far today and are weary.”
“It’s late,” said Gaius, “so we can’t very well go out to find food; but what we have, you’re welcome to, if that will content you.”
“We’ll be content with whatever you have in the house; for I’ve proved you before, and you’re never without what is needed.”

Then he went down and spoke to the cook, whose name was Taste-that-which-is-good, to get supper ready for so many pilgrims. That done, he came up again and said, “Come, my good friends, you are welcome here, and I’m glad I have a house to entertain you in. While supper is being made ready, let us entertain one another with some good talk, if you please.”
They all said, “Agreed.”
“Whose wife is this aged matron?” asked Gaius. “And whose daughter is this young woman?”

“The woman is the wife of one Christian, a pilgrim of former times,” said Great-heart, “and these are his four children. The young woman is a friend of hers, one she has persuaded to come with her on pilgrimage. The boys all take after their father and long to tread in his steps; indeed, if they so much as see a place where the old pilgrim once lay, or any print of his foot, it brings joy to their hearts, and they want to lie or tread in the same spot.”

“Is this Christian’s wife?” said Gaius. “And are these Christian’s children? I knew your husband’s father, yes, and his father’s father. Many of this stock have been good; their ancestors first lived at Antioch. [Acts 11:26] Christian’s forebears, as I suppose you’ve heard your husband say, were very worthy men. More than any I know, they showed themselves men of great virtue and courage for the Lord of pilgrims, for his ways, and for those who loved him. I have heard of many of your husband’s relations who stood every trial for the sake of the truth. Stephen, one of the first of the family your husband sprang from, was stoned to death. [Acts 7:59-60] James, another of that generation, was killed with the edge of the sword. [Acts 12:2] To say nothing of Paul and Peter, men anciently of the same family, there was Ignatius, who was thrown to the lions; Romanus, whose flesh was cut from his bones in pieces; and Polycarp, who played the man in the fire. There was the one who was hung up in a basket in the sun for the wasps to eat, and the one they put in a sack and threw into the sea to drown. It would be quite impossible to count up all of that family who have suffered injury and death for the love of a pilgrim’s life. And I can’t help being glad to see that your husband has left four such boys as these behind him. I hope they will carry on their father’s name, tread in their father’s steps, and come to their father’s end.”
“Indeed, sir, they are likely lads,” said Great-heart. “They seem to choose their father’s ways with all their hearts.”

“That’s what I said; and so Christian’s family is likely to spread abroad over the face of the ground, and to be numerous on the face of the earth. So let Christiana look out some young women for her sons, to whom they may be betrothed, so that the name of their father and the house of his forebears may never be forgotten in the world.”
“It would be a pity for this family to fall and die out,” said Honest.

“Fall it cannot, but shrink it may,” said Gaius. “Let Christiana take my advice; that is the way to keep it up. And Christiana,” said the innkeeper, “I’m glad to see you and your friend Mercy here together, a lovely pair. If I may advise you, bring Mercy into a nearer relation to you. If she is willing, let her be given to Matthew, your eldest son; that is the way to secure you a posterity on the earth.”
So this match was agreed on, and in due course they were married; but more of that later.

Gaius went on: “Now I will speak on behalf of women, to take away their reproach. For as death and the curse came into the world by a woman [Gen. 3], so also did life and health: ‘God sent forth his Son, made of a woman.’ [Gal. 4:4] Indeed, to show how much those who came after abhorred the act of the first mother, the women of the Old Testament longed for children, in case this one or that one might happen to be the mother of the Savior of the world.

“I will say again that when the Savior had come, women rejoiced in him before either man or angel. [Luke 2] I don’t read that any man ever gave Christ so much as a penny; but women followed him and ministered to him out of their own substance. [Luke 8:2-3] It was a woman who washed his feet with tears, and a woman who anointed his body for burial. [Luke 7:37, 50; John 11:2; 12:3] It was women who wept when he was going to the Cross, women who followed him from the Cross, and women who sat by his tomb when he was buried. [Luke 23:27; Matt. 27:55-56, 61] Women were the first with him on the morning of his resurrection, and women first brought word to his disciples that he had risen from the dead. [Luke 24:22-23] Women, then, are highly favored, and show by all this that they share with us in the grace of life.”
Now the cook sent up word that supper was almost ready, and sent someone to lay the cloth and the plates, and to set the salt and bread in order.
“The sight of this cloth,” said Matthew, “and of this forerunner of supper, gives me a bigger appetite for my food than I had before.”

“In the same way,” said Gaius, “let every teaching that ministers to you in this life beget in you a greater desire to sit at the supper of the great King in his kingdom. For all the preaching, books, and ordinances here are only the laying of the plates and the setting of salt on the board, compared with the feast our Lord will make for us when we come to his house.”

So supper came up. First a heave-shoulder and a wave-breast were set on the table before them [Lev. 7:32-34; 10:14-15], to show that they must begin their meal with prayer and praise to God. [Ps. 25:1; Heb. 13:15] With the heave-shoulder David lifted his heart up to God; and the wave-breast, where his heart lay, he used to lean on his harp when he played. These two dishes were very fresh and good, and they all ate heartily.

Next they brought up a bottle of wine, red as blood. [Deut. 32:14] “Drink freely,” said Gaius. “This is the juice of the true vine, which makes glad the heart of God and man.” [Judg. 9:13; John 15:1] So they drank and were merry.

Next came a dish of milk with bread crumbled in it. “Let the boys have that,” said Gaius, “so they may grow by it.” [1 Pet. 2:1-2] Then they brought up in turn a dish of butter and honey. “Eat freely of this,” said Gaius, “for it is good to cheer and strengthen your judgment and understanding. This was our Lord’s dish when he was a child: ‘Butter and honey shall he eat, that he may know to refuse the evil and choose the good.’” [Isa. 7:15]
Then they brought them a dish of apples, very good-tasting fruit. “May we eat apples,” said Matthew, “when it was with apples like these that the serpent deceived our first mother?”
Then Gaius said:

v: Apples they were by which we were beguiled;
yet sin, not apples, has our souls defiled.
Forbidden apples, eaten, taint the blood;
to eat what is commanded does us good.
Drink of his flagons, then, you church, his dove,
and eat his apples, you who are sick with love.

blocks.p: “I raised the question,” said Matthew, “because a while ago I was sick from eating fruit.”
“Forbidden fruit will make you sick,” said Gaius, “but not what our Lord has allowed.”

While they were talking like this, another dish was set before them, a dish of nuts. [Song 6:11] Some at the table said, “Nuts spoil tender teeth, especially children’s teeth.” When Gaius heard that, he said:

v: Hard texts are nuts (I will not call them cheaters)
whose shells keep back their kernels from the eaters.
Open the shells, and you will have the meat;
they’re set before you here to crack and eat.

blocks.p: Then they were very merry, and sat a long time at the table talking of many things. “My good landlord,” said the old gentleman, “while we are cracking your nuts, open this riddle for us, if you please:

v: A man there was, though some did count him mad,
the more he cast away, the more he had.”

blocks.p: They all paid close attention, wondering what good Gaius would say. He sat still a while, and then replied:

v: He who bestows his goods upon the poor
shall have as much again, and ten times more.

blocks.p: “I must say, sir,” said Joseph, “I didn’t think you could have found it out.”

“Oh,” said Gaius, “I have been trained in this way a long while. Nothing teaches like experience. I’ve learned from my Lord to be kind, and found by experience that I have gained by it. ‘There is one who scatters, and yet increases; and there is one who withholds more than is right, but it tends to poverty.’ [Prov. 11:24] ‘There is one who makes himself rich, yet has nothing; and one who makes himself poor, yet has great riches.’” [Prov. 13:7]
Then Samuel whispered to Christiana his mother, “Mother, this is a very good man’s house. Let us stay here a good while, and let my brother Matthew be married to Mercy here before we go any further.”
Gaius the host overheard him. “With a very good will, my child,” he said.

So they stayed there more than a month, and Mercy was given to Matthew as his wife. While they stayed, Mercy, as her custom was, kept making coats and clothes to give to the poor, and by this she won a very good name for the pilgrims.

But to return to our story. After supper the lads asked for a bed, since they were tired from traveling; and Gaius called for someone to show them their room. “I will put them to bed,” said Mercy. So she took them to bed, and they slept well; but the rest sat up all night, for Gaius and they were such suitable company that they could not bring themselves to part. After much talk about their Lord, themselves, and their journey, old Mr. Honest, who had put the riddle to Gaius, began to nod.
“What, sir, are you getting drowsy?” said Great-heart. “Come, rouse yourself; here’s a riddle for you.”
“Let’s hear it,” said Mr. Honest. Then said Great-heart:

v: He who would kill must first be overcome;
who would live abroad must first die at home.

blocks.p: “Ha!” said Mr. Honest. “That’s a hard one: hard to explain, and harder to practice. But come, landlord,” he said, “if you please, I’ll leave my part to you. You explain it, and I’ll hear what you say.”
“No,” said Gaius. “It was put to you, and it’s expected you should answer it.”
Then the old gentleman said:

v: By grace a man must conquered be
before his sin he slays;
and he who’d prove he lives to me
must die to his own ways.

blocks.p: “That’s right,” said Gaius. “Good doctrine and experience both teach it. For first, until grace shows itself and overcomes the soul with its glory, the soul has no heart at all to oppose sin; besides, if sin is Satan’s cords, by which the soul lies bound, how should it resist before it is loosed from that weakness? Second, no one who knows either reason or grace will believe that a man can be a living monument of grace while he is a slave to his own corruptions.

“And now that it comes to mind, I’ll tell you a story worth hearing. There were two men who went on pilgrimage; one began when he was young, the other when he was old. The young man had strong corruptions to grapple with; the old man’s had decayed with the decay of nature. The young man trod his steps as evenly as the old one did, and was every bit as light. Now which of them had his graces shining clearest, since both seemed alike?”

“The young man’s, without a doubt,” said Honest. “For whatever holds out against the greatest opposition gives the best proof that it is strongest, especially when it keeps pace with what meets not half so much opposition, as old age certainly does not. Besides, I’ve noticed that old men have congratulated themselves by this mistake, taking the decay of nature for a gracious conquest over their corruptions, and so have been apt to deceive themselves. Indeed, old men who are gracious are best able to give advice to the young, because they have seen most of the emptiness of things. But still, when an old man and a young one set out together, the young one has the advantage of the clearest showing of a work of grace within him, though the old man’s corruptions are naturally the weakest.”

So they sat talking until daybreak. When the household was up, Christiana told her son James to read a chapter, and he read the fifty-third of Isaiah. When he had finished, Mr. Honest asked why it was said that the Savior would come “out of a dry ground,” and that “he had no form or comeliness.”

“To the first,” said Great-heart, “I answer: because the church of the Jews, from which Christ came, had by then lost almost all the sap and spirit of religion. To the second I say: the words are spoken in the person of unbelievers, who, because they lack the eye that can see into our Prince’s heart, judge him by the plainness of his outside. They are like people who don’t know that precious stones come covered in a homely crust, and who, when they find one, throw it away again as men do a common stone, because they don’t know what they have found.”

“Well,” said Gaius, “now that you’re here, and since I know Mr. Great-heart is good with his weapons, if you like, after we’ve refreshed ourselves we’ll walk into the fields and see whether we can do any good. About a mile from here there is a giant called Slay-good, who does great harm along the King’s highway in these parts, and I know where his haunt is. He is master of a gang of thieves; it would be a good thing if we could clear these parts of him.”

So they agreed, and went: Mr. Great-heart with his sword, helmet, and shield, and the rest with spears and staves. When they came to the place where he was, they found him with one Feeble-mind in his hands, whom his servants had brought to him after catching him on the road. The giant was now rifling his pockets, meaning afterward to pick his bones, for he was of the flesh-eating kind.
